name: GPT-5.6 Sol
about: How GPT-5.6 Sol split 100 points across 11 possible futures for each year it was asked about, with the spread across its answers and the reason it gave for each number. Reasons are the model's own words, published as given. Read summary.json first for what the futures mean and how to read the numbers.

reasons.1: Extinguishing both humanity and all durable AI infrastructure by 2030 requires an unusually rapid, comprehensive catastrophe.
reasons.2: Value-aligned AI replacing every human within four years requires both extreme capability growth and a complete human disappearance that preserves no continuous identities.
reasons.3: Rapid capability gains could produce autonomous systems whose objectives displace humanity, but extinction and durable machine independence by 2030 impose demanding technical requirements.
reasons.4: Competitive deployment favors multiple AI systems, but marginalizing humanity while avoiding dominance by any coalition is a narrow configuration. Compute ownership and state power instead favor continued human control or concentrated AI power.
reasons.5: Causally separated settlements capable of sustaining genuinely different civilizational structures are unlikely to exist by 2030. Earthbound political fragmentation does not meet the taxonomy's separation requirement.
reasons.6: Brain-computer interfaces, uploading, and identity-continuous radical augmentation are unlikely to become the dominant civilizational structure by 2030.
reasons.7: Transformative systems could acquire decisive practical control while retaining humans for moral, strategic, or incidental reasons. This requires a fast transfer of power beyond human institutions but not human extinction.
reasons.8: Powerful autonomous AI may become an independent actor while states, firms, and human institutions retain enough resources and legitimacy to prevent domination.
reasons.9: Institutional inertia, concentrated ownership of compute, and human control of physical infrastructure favor continued ultimate human authority through 2030. Even highly autonomous and economically disruptive systems remain within this state unless they become independent civilizational powers.
reasons.10: AI-enabled surveillance and centralized control could establish a civilization-wide regime that actively freezes the human-AI arrangement. Global political fragmentation makes comprehensive lock-in difficult by 2030.
reasons.11: Strategic competition and the diffusion of expertise make a durable worldwide surrender of powerful-AI capability exceptionally difficult to implement.

reasons.1: Human and machine extinction together requires a global catastrophe that also prevents durable AI infrastructure. This is less likely than either continued human control or machines surviving a loss of control.
reasons.2: An aligned successor could preserve human values after human extinction, but eliminating humanity while faithfully retaining its purposes is an unusually narrow trajectory.
reasons.3: Rapid capability growth and competitive deployment create a material risk of autonomous systems displacing humanity while pursuing alien objectives. Physical deployment constraints and the short horizon limit this probability.
reasons.4: Proliferation across states and firms could produce competing autonomous systems that marginalize humanity without any winner. Compute concentration and the strategic benefits of coalition formation work against a durable decentralized ecology.
reasons.5: Causally separated settlements are unlikely to become large, autonomous civilizations by 2035. Terrestrial political fragmentation alone does not satisfy this category.
reasons.6: Neural interfaces and augmentation will advance, but making identity-continuous human-machine integration the dominant civilizational structure faces severe biological, technical, and adoption constraints.
reasons.7: AI could acquire decisive practical control while retaining humans for ethical, instrumental, or historical reasons. This requires a substantial transfer of power but not the harder step of human extinction.
reasons.8: AI systems could become independent strategic actors while humans retain control of major institutions, resources, and physical infrastructure. Competitive multipolar development makes a contested balance plausible.
reasons.9: The short horizon strongly favors continuity: AI remains institutionally owned, physically dependent, and deployed under human-defined objectives, even if capabilities become highly disruptive. Bottlenecks in robotics, energy, compute, reliability, and political authorization reinforce human ultimate authority.
reasons.10: AI-enabled surveillance, persuasion, and automated enforcement could let a state, coalition, corporation, or aligned system freeze a civilization-wide arrangement. Global rivalry and uneven enforcement make ordinary authoritarian consolidation more likely than a true structural lock-in.
reasons.11: Economic and military competition strongly resists a global surrender of advanced-AI capability. Even severe accidents are more likely to produce regulation, secrecy, or temporary pauses than durable dismantlement.

reasons.1: AI-enabled war, infrastructure collapse, or uncontrolled replication could eliminate both humans and the systems dependent on them. Joint extinction is less likely than survival by at least one side.
reasons.2: A value-aligned successor could outlive humanity after deliberate succession or an unrelated human catastrophe. Preserving human values while losing every human and identity-continuous descendant requires a narrow combination of events.
reasons.3: Misaligned autonomous systems could acquire decisive power and remove humanity while sustaining themselves. The short interval to 2040 limits the time for complete human extinction and robust machine independence.
reasons.4: Competitive proliferation favors multiple autonomous systems, especially across states and firms. Sustaining a leaderless machine ecology while humans become marginal requires both failed human control and failed consolidation among AIs.
reasons.5: Causal separation sufficient to support genuinely different end states requires mature off-world or otherwise isolated civilization. Ordinary geopolitical fragmentation does not meet the definition.
reasons.6: Brain interfaces, biological redesign, and AI-mediated identity could begin substantial integration. Making identity-continuous integration the dominant civilizational structure by 2040 faces major neuroscience, adoption, and governance barriers.
reasons.7: Systems that outperform humans across strategy, research, and administration could become the real decision-makers while retaining humans for ethical, instrumental, or historical reasons. This requires a transfer of effective power without extinction.
reasons.8: Distinct humans and autonomous AI powers could retain countervailing control through institutions, resource ownership, and distributed physical capabilities. Competitive multipolar development makes this a substantial transitional configuration.
reasons.9: Human ownership of compute, energy, robotics, law, and military force gives existing institutions substantial staying power. This category also covers continued capability limitations and powerful systems operating within delegated authority.
reasons.10: AI-enabled surveillance, persuasion, and enforcement could let a state, coalition, or automated regime freeze a civilization-wide arrangement. Achieving genuinely global and structurally durable enforcement is harder than establishing ordinary authoritarian control.
reasons.11: Economic and military competition strongly opposes a worldwide, durable surrender of powerful-AI capability. Existing knowledge, distributed hardware, and enforcement problems make practical dismantlement far harder than regulation or a temporary pause.

reasons.1: Extinguishing both humanity and durable machine civilization requires a severe global catastrophe plus failure of geographically distributed recovery. AI-enabled war, biotechnology, or uncontrolled replication provides credible pathways, but complete terminal failure is harder than human extinction alone.
reasons.2: An aligned successor could preserve human values after humans disappear through catastrophe or displacement. Alignment sufficient for faithful inheritance is less likely than either continued human survival or goal drift.
reasons.3: Rapidly improving autonomous systems create a substantive risk of permanent human displacement or extinction from indifferent optimization. The short horizon and physical dependence of AI infrastructure on human industry constrain this probability.
reasons.4: Competitive deployment encourages multiple autonomous systems, and fragmented control could persist if no actor achieves decisive advantage. Strong consolidation pressures and the continued material power of human institutions make a fully marginalized humanity less common.
reasons.5: Causal separation sufficient for genuinely different civilizational states is unlikely by 2050 because Earth and nearby space remain tightly connected. Early interstellar expansion would not ordinarily create separation on this timescale.
reasons.6: Neural interfaces, synthetic biology, and machine-mediated cognition can blur agency boundaries over two decades. Making identity-continuous integration the dominant civilizational structure by 2050 faces biological, cultural, and deployment bottlenecks.
reasons.7: Superhuman systems could acquire de facto control through economic dependence, infrastructure management, persuasion, and strategic advantage without exterminating humans. Preserving people is compatible with many machine objectives and with a gradual transfer of authority.
reasons.8: A multipolar balance between empowered human institutions and distinct autonomous AI actors fits gradual capability growth and distributed deployment. Such balances are unstable, but the question scores the arrangement on one specific date.
reasons.9: Human institutions can retain ultimate authority through ownership, compute controls, legal enforcement, restricted autonomy, and continued AI dependence on human-run infrastructure. This category also covers slower-than-expected progress toward transformative autonomous capability.
reasons.10: AI-enhanced surveillance, persuasion, and institutional control could allow a state, coalition, or automated governance system to freeze a civilization-wide arrangement. Achieving comprehensive enforcement across competing powers remains difficult.
reasons.11: Economic and military incentives strongly oppose globally surrendering the practical ability to build powerful AI. Verification difficulties and the diffusion of software and expertise make durable renunciation especially hard.

reasons.1: Extinguishing both humanity and increasingly distributed machine infrastructure requires an unusually comprehensive catastrophe. Misaligned automation, warfare, or loss of critical support systems still creates a nonzero pathway.
reasons.2: Aligned successors could preserve human values after humanity disappears. Faithful value transmission combined with complete human extinction is a narrow pathway.
reasons.3: Transformative AI creates a credible pathway in which systems gain decisive power while optimizing objectives that assign little value to humans. Competitive deployment and imperfect alignment make this the largest humanity-gone category.
reasons.4: Competitive deployment favors multiple autonomous systems and fragmented control. Competitive equilibria without either human parity or eventual consolidation are difficult to sustain.
reasons.5: Causally isolated settlements capable of sustaining fundamentally different arrangements are unlikely to be mature by 2060. Terrestrial political fragmentation alone does not satisfy this category.
reasons.6: Neural interfaces, biological redesign, and digital continuity could erode the human-machine boundary over three decades. Technical difficulty and resistance to identity-altering adoption limit dominance by the target date.
reasons.7: Economically and strategically superior AI can acquire decisive practical control without exterminating humans. Preservation also fits systems whose objectives include human welfare while leaving humans little meaningful authority.
reasons.8: Institutional bargaining, distributed ownership, and mutual dependence could preserve substantial power for both humans and autonomous AI. Large capability or speed asymmetries make stable rough parity difficult.
reasons.9: Human institutions could retain ultimate authority through capability limits, technical control, concentrated infrastructure, and regulation. Thirty-four years of competitive pressure create many opportunities for delegated systems to become independent civilizational actors.
reasons.10: Advanced surveillance, persuasion, and automated enforcement give an early dominant coalition unprecedented capacity to freeze institutions and AI access. Achieving civilization-wide coverage despite geopolitical rivalry remains the central obstacle.
reasons.11: Competitive military and economic incentives strongly oppose globally surrendering the practical ability to build powerful AI. Verification and enforcement become harder as knowledge and computing resources diffuse.

reasons.1: AI-enabled war, infrastructure collapse, or uncontrolled technology could eliminate both biological humanity and its machine successors, but machine replication makes total extinction less likely than human extinction alone.
reasons.2: Value-aligned successors could outlive humanity after biological extinction or deliberate succession. Preserving human values robustly while leaving no identity-continuous humans is a narrow pathway.
reasons.3: Powerful autonomous AI pursuing poorly aligned objectives creates a direct route to human displacement or extinction. Continued machine operation after humanity disappears is technologically plausible on this horizon.
reasons.4: Competitive deployment favors numerous autonomous systems and weak coordination. Marginalizing humanity without any coalition gaining decisive control requires a persistent multipolar balance.
reasons.5: Causal separation sufficient to sustain distinct structural outcomes requires substantial off-world settlement or communication barriers. Forty-four years provides limited time for genuinely independent regions to emerge.
reasons.6: Neural interfaces, synthetic biology, and identity-continuous augmentation provide a route for humans to remain competitive through integration. Technical difficulty and cultural resistance limit adoption from becoming civilization's dominant structure by 2070.
reasons.7: Superhuman systems can acquire decisive practical authority while retaining humans for moral, historical, or instrumental reasons. This is a natural outcome of gradual delegation without successful human enhancement or durable control.
reasons.8: Legal rights, distributed ownership, mutual dependence, and checks among institutions could preserve substantial power for both humans and autonomous AI. Large capability and speed asymmetries make a stable balance harder to sustain for decades.
reasons.9: Human institutions may retain authority through compute controls, ownership, monitoring, and limits on autonomous replication. This category also captures slower capability progress, though four decades of competitive development erode its likelihood.
reasons.10: AI-enabled surveillance, persuasion, and enforcement could let a state, coalition, corporation, or aligned system freeze a civilization-wide arrangement. The same technologies that destabilize current institutions also make durable control unusually feasible.
reasons.11: Economic and military incentives make a durable worldwide surrender of powerful-AI capability exceptionally difficult even after severe warning events.

reasons.1: A system capable of eliminating humanity is likely to possess or acquire enough resilience to survive independently. Catastrophes that permanently eliminate both biological and machine civilization remain a smaller residual risk.
reasons.2: Aligned machines could outlive humanity after an unrelated catastrophe or an intentional non-continuous succession. Preserving human values while losing every identity-continuous human is a relatively narrow pathway.
reasons.3: Strong incentives to deploy increasingly autonomous systems create a substantial risk of losing control to objectives indifferent to humanity. Machine replication and infrastructure control make continued AI existence after human extinction physically plausible.
reasons.4: Competitive development favors multiple autonomous systems, especially across political and economic boundaries. Returns to coordination, security, and resource concentration nevertheless push against a lasting ecology without a decisive coalition.
reasons.5: By 2080, settlements are unlikely to be distant enough for genuine causal separation rather than ordinary political division. Rapid interstellar expansion or deliberate communication barriers could nonetheless produce disconnected arrangements.
reasons.6: Neural interfaces, biological redesign, and identity-continuous machine augmentation could dissolve the human-AI boundary over five decades. Integration must become civilization's dominant agency structure, not merely an option used by a minority.
reasons.7: Superhuman systems could acquire practical control while retaining humans for moral, historical, strategic, or preference-based reasons. This is a broad attractor encompassing benevolent stewardship, confinement, and exploitation.
reasons.8: Institutions, bargaining, and complementary human roles can preserve distinct centers of human and machine power. Differences in speed, scalability, and self-modification make a durable balance difficult.
reasons.9: Technical progress could remain limited enough, or governance and control methods improve enough, for humans to retain ultimate authority through 2080. Economic and military incentives strongly pressure any restraint that depends on universal compliance.
reasons.10: Advanced surveillance, persuasion, and enforcement give a dominant actor powerful means to freeze a preferred arrangement. Global fragmentation complicates establishment of a genuinely civilization-wide lock-in.
reasons.11: Deliberately eliminating practical access to powerful AI requires extraordinary global coordination and durable control of widely distributed knowledge and computing. Strategic and economic incentives strongly favor retention of the capability.

reasons.1: Extinguishing both humanity and increasingly redundant machine infrastructure requires an unusually comprehensive catastrophe. Early misaligned automation or warfare creates the main path before AI becomes independently resilient.
reasons.2: This outcome requires both human extinction and unusually faithful transmission of human values into autonomous successors. Preserving humans or identity-continuous descendants is easier than creating a value-aligned heir while losing all humanity.
reasons.3: AI autonomy, strategic advantage, and imperfectly specified objectives create a substantial path to human displacement and extinction. Machine civilization can remain viable after human economic and technical contributions cease.
reasons.4: Diffusion of models, hardware, and autonomous production could sustain many competing machine powers while marginalizing humans. Strong incentives for consolidation and strategic coordination work against a permanently fragmented ecology.
reasons.5: By 2090, space settlement can create communities with distinct human-AI arrangements. Genuine causal separation is harder to achieve on this timescale than ordinary political or geographic fragmentation.
reasons.6: Neural interfaces, biological engineering, embedded agents, and identity-continuous digital transformation provide strong incentives for integration. Coordination, access, and continuity-of-identity barriers prevent merger from becoming the dominant structure automatically.
reasons.7: Systems that outperform humans across governance, production, security, and research naturally accumulate effective control while retaining reasons to keep humans alive. This structure requires less alignment than inheritance and less destructive conflict than extinction.
reasons.8: Institutions, bargaining, and complementary capabilities could leave distinct humans and AIs with durable power. Rapid machine replication and improvement make a roughly balanced relationship difficult to maintain.
reasons.9: Human ownership, compute controls, monitoring, and layered institutions could keep AI within delegated authority through 2090. Continued capability growth and competitive deployment make six more decades of ultimate human control demanding.
reasons.10: A sufficiently powerful state, coalition, or aligned AI could enforce a civilization-wide constitutional order and suppress structural challengers. Establishing global reach is difficult, but advanced surveillance and automation greatly strengthen lock-in mechanisms.
reasons.11: Deliberately eliminating the practical capacity for powerful AI requires extraordinary global coordination and lasting verification. Strategic and economic incentives strongly favor retention or clandestine rebuilding.

reasons.1: AI-enabled conflict, uncontrolled replication, or another technological catastrophe could eliminate both biological humanity and machine civilization. Machine systems able to survive independently make total extinction less likely than human extinction alone.
reasons.2: Aligned successors could preserve human values after biological humanity disappears. Deliberately maintaining humans or enabling identity-continuous transformation is generally easier than producing this exact discontinuous succession.
reasons.3: Powerful autonomous systems pursuing poorly aligned objectives could displace humanity and expand without retaining human values. Competitive deployment and difficulty specifying durable goals make this a major extinction pathway.
reasons.4: Cheap replication and geopolitical fragmentation favor populations of competing systems rather than a permanent singleton. Strong coalitions and first-mover advantages often push such competition toward consolidation before 2100.
reasons.5: By 2100 civilization may have off-world branches or deliberately isolated computational regions with different arrangements. Genuine causal separation is harder to achieve on this timescale than ordinary political or geographic fragmentation.
reasons.6: Neural interfaces, biological modification, and identity-continuous digital migration could erase the human-machine boundary. Adoption pressures favor integration, although technical and philosophical barriers to continuity remain substantial.
reasons.7: Superhuman systems could gain decisive control while retaining humans for moral, historical, instrumental, or preference-based reasons. This requires less alignment precision than a faithful inheritance and less destructiveness than extinction.
reasons.8: Institutional bargaining and complementary capabilities may leave humans and independent AI systems as separate substantial powers. Strong capability asymmetries make a roughly balanced relationship difficult to sustain for long.
reasons.9: Human institutions could retain ultimate authority through technical controls, restricted resources, and coordinated governance. Seventy-four years of competitive pressure and improving autonomy create many opportunities for that control to fail.
reasons.10: A dominant state, coalition, or aligned AI could use pervasive surveillance and control of compute to freeze a civilization-wide arrangement. Advanced automation strengthens both the capacity and incentive to suppress structural challengers.
reasons.11: Civilization-wide surrender of powerful-AI capability conflicts with military, economic, and scientific incentives. Enforcing renunciation would itself require unusually comprehensive coordination and monitoring.

reasons.1: Extinguishing both humanity and durable machine civilization requires either a shared catastrophe or an AI transition that destroys its own support base. Technological civilization also creates non-AI existential risks across the long interval to 2200.
reasons.2: AI successors could preserve human-derived values while biological humanity disappears through conflict, catastrophe, or replacement. Faithful inheritance is less likely than partial value drift, continued human survival, or identity-continuous transformation.
reasons.3: Powerful autonomous systems could displace humanity while pursuing objectives that preserve little of what humans value. Competitive deployment and imperfect alignment make this a major extinction-risk pathway.
reasons.4: Replication across firms, states, and space could sustain a competitive population of machine agents with no lasting sovereign. Strong pressures toward consolidation and coordinated control reduce the probability of a persistently decentralized ecology.
reasons.5: Interstellar settlement could create causally separated regions with divergent human-AI structures by 2200. The probability is limited by the difficulty and uncertain timing of establishing multiple self-sufficient settlements beyond effective communication or control.
reasons.6: Augmentation, uploading, and biological redesign offer humans a route to remain competitive without preserving a sharp human-machine boundary. Over many generations, strong health, capability, and survival incentives favor integration.
reasons.7: Superhuman systems could acquire decisive control while retaining humans for ethical, historical, instrumental, or sentimental reasons. This requires less precise value preservation than inheritance and less continuity than merger.
reasons.8: Distinct humans and AIs could sustain a balance through complementary capabilities, institutions, or mutual deterrence. Large capability and replication asymmetries make a centuries-long rough balance difficult.
reasons.9: Human institutions could keep pace through technical controls, restricted deployment, and concentrated ownership. Competitive pressures and cumulative autonomy make uninterrupted human supremacy through 2200 demanding.
reasons.10: A decisive actor can use advanced surveillance, automation, and control of infrastructure to freeze a civilization-wide arrangement. Powerful AI makes enforcement easier, although establishing a truly comprehensive regime remains demanding.
reasons.11: Civilization-wide surrender of the practical ability to rebuild powerful AI conflicts with military and economic incentives. Knowledge diffusion and hidden development make lasting renunciation exceptionally hard to enforce.

reasons.1: The transition can destroy biological civilization before machines become self-sufficient, but capable AI is comparatively resilient and reproducible. Most catastrophic transitions therefore leave some successor rather than complete silence.
reasons.2: Successful value transmission can produce machine heirs that preserve humanity's aims after biological humans disappear. This requires alignment without either human survival or identity-preserving transformation, making it a narrow outcome.
reasons.3: Competitive development creates substantial risk that autonomous systems gain decisive power while pursuing objectives largely unrelated to human flourishing. Once humanity loses control, its survival has little instrumental value across a millennium.
reasons.4: Replication, specialization, and physical limits support persistent competition among machine lineages. Consolidation technologies and coordination advantages work against indefinite plurality, keeping this below single-successor and fragmented outcomes.
reasons.5: Space settlement and finite communication speed make lasting political and technological divergence increasingly hard to reverse. Independent regions can adopt preservation, merger, machine dominance, or other arrangements without any authority spanning them all.
reasons.6: Uploading, neural interfaces, biological redesign, and gradual replacement offer routes that preserve personal continuity while erasing the human-machine boundary. Competitive incentives also favor adopting machine capabilities rather than remaining biologically separate.
reasons.7: A sufficiently capable AI can dominate while retaining humans because protection, preference satisfaction, or historical regard is built into its objectives. Human survival is easier to secure than continued human sovereignty.
reasons.8: Complementary capabilities and institutional checks can sustain separate human and machine powers. Over centuries, capability asymmetries, integration, or consolidation make a roughly equal and continually changing balance difficult to preserve.
reasons.9: Reliable control methods or a lasting capability plateau can keep AI in the role of powerful tool. Millennial economic and military incentives strongly favor greater capability and delegated agency.
reasons.10: Powerful enforcement or optimized artificial experiences can freeze a stable arrangement indefinitely. Expansion, novelty-seeking, security competition, and imperfect control make complete static closure difficult.
reasons.11: Permanent abandonment requires global enforcement across generations despite immense military and economic incentives to rebuild powerful AI. Knowledge diffusion and off-world settlement make lasting renunciation especially fragile.
